verdict.rationale: Temporal ships first-party Schedules that start Workflow Executions at specific times, with durable execution that resumes after crashes and retries failed Activities automatically, so automations, including LLM agent loops, run unattended in the background. Community users report running alert-handling, provisioning and Reverse ETL systems on it. Missing for 10: automations must be authored as code and run on Workers the user deploys (only partly offset by Serverless Workers); schedule configuration depth (recurrence options, pause/backfill) is thinly evidenced; no independent hands-on report of recurring scheduled runs specifically.

support.subject: As an AI-native user, I can set up automations that run autonomously in the background

citations.quote: A Schedule contains instructions for starting a Workflow Execution at specific times.
Temporal delivers crash-proof execution by guaranteeing that applications resume exactly where they left off after crashes, network failures, or infrastructure outages
a Workflow resumes automatically after a crash, a network timeout, or a multi-day wait for a human to approve a step
Temporal's default behavior is to automatically retry an Activity that fails, so transient or intermittent failures require no action on your part.
Long-running, stateful agent loops that call LLMs and tools, wait on humans, and pick up exactly where they left off after a failure.
I'm doing a lot of work with alert handling and provisioning systems using Temporal.
